name: Specialty Beer
title: Specialty Beer: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Specialty beer explained: the home for beers brewed with unusual ingredients or methods, and how to judge one fairly.
tagline: The open category for beers that use an ingredient or method no other style has a name for.
tastes:
Specialty beer is the drawer for everything that does not fit elsewhere. It covers beers brewed with an unusual fermentable such as rice, honey, maple or jaggery, beers built around a spice or flower, and beers made with an unusual process. Because it is a catch all, it has no single taste. A saffron lager and a 15 percent barley wine both belong.

What holds it together is a way of judging. A specialty beer should taste like a good base beer plus the thing on the label, and the special ingredient should be clearly there without bullying the rest. If a brewer says tulsi, you should find tulsi. If you only find tulsi, the beer has failed.

That makes the category a playground for brewpubs. It is where you find beers made with local produce, odd sugars and family recipes, and where a brewer shows whether they understand balance or are just chasing novelty.

profile.look: Any colour, clarity or head, set by the base beer. Some special ingredients tint the beer, as saffron does gold or hibiscus does pink.
profile.aroma_flavour: A recognisable base style plus a clear, identifiable special ingredient or process character. The two should read as one beer, not two flavours side by side.
profile.mouthfeel: Set by the base style, from light and spritzy to thick and warming. Added sugars can thin the body; lactose or oats fill it out.
profile.ingredients: A conventional malt, hop and yeast base, plus the defining addition: unusual grains, honey, jaggery, maple, spices, flowers, tea, or a special process such as wood ageing.

in_india: This is where Indian brewers have the most to say. Saffron, kokum, tulsi, gondhoraj lime, jaggery, black rice and Darjeeling tea have all found their way into beers here, and a local ingredient gives a brewery something an import cannot copy. Ask what the base beer is before you order, because a specialty beer can be anything from a light lager to a strong ale. Delicate spices and flowers fade in heat, so drink these fresh.

pairings.why: A saffron or spice led specialty beer echoes the fennel and dry ginger, and stays light enough for the yoghurt gravy.
Smoky, lightly spiced paneer is a forgiving partner for most specialty beers and lets the special ingredient show.
A tart, fruited specialty beer cuts the vinegar and chilli heat.
Saffron and milk sweetness meet a saffron or honey beer and make the shared ingredient obvious.
